title: THE UNTOLD STORY OF EGLAH
paragraphs: Some names in Scripture thunder across history.
Others appear almost unnoticed, like a single footprint in the sand before the tide comes in.
Eglah is one of those names.
She appears only briefly in the biblical record, mentioned almost as an afterthought among King David's wives:
"His sixth son was Ithream, by Eglah David's wife." (2 Samuel 3:5)
And yet Scripture never wastes words.
Every name preserved by the Holy Spirit exists for a reason.
Some stories are written in paragraphs.
This is the untold story hidden behind one of the Bible's quietest women.
And it may be far more relevant to your life than you realize.
Because many people know exactly what it feels like to be an Eglah.
Standing in the shadows while everyone else seems to occupy center stage.
Yet throughout Scripture, God repeatedly reveals a stunning truth:
He specializes in seeing the people nobody else notices.
The Hebrew name עֶגְלָה (Eglah) literally means "heifer" or "young cow."
To modern ears, that sounds strange.
But within the ancient Hebrew world, names often carried symbolic beauty, vitality, fertility, strength, and value.
They reflected hopes, circumstances, character, or prophetic significance.
What we know with certainty is remarkably little.
Eglah was one of David's wives.
She is listed sixth among the wives mentioned during David's reign in Hebron.
That is the extent of the biblical record.
And perhaps that silence itself carries a lesson.
Modern culture teaches us that significance is measured by visibility.
The Kingdom of God measures differently.
Heaven has never confused prominence with importance.
Many of God's most treasured servants occupy only a few verses.
Yet they remain eternally known by God.
One of the most beautiful titles of God appears in the story of Hagar.
After being abandoned and afflicted, she encounters God in the wilderness and declares:
Not merely a God who sees nations.
Not merely a God who sees kings.
The Hebrew verb רָאָה (ra'ah) means to see, perceive, understand, notice, and attend to.
God's seeing is never passive observation.
This truth changes everything about Eglah.
History may know almost nothing about her.
Some people reading this are exhausted from living unseen lives.
The God who saw Hagar also saw Eglah.
Eglah's story becomes even more intriguing when viewed within the complicated realities surrounding David's family.
The years in Hebron were not simple years.
David was a man after God's own heart, yet he was also a deeply flawed man.
The household surrounding him reflected both divine blessing and human brokenness.
This is one reason Scripture feels so real.
The Bible never airbrushes its heroes.
And that honesty points us directly toward the Gospel.
Because Scripture is not ultimately about impressive people.
It is about a perfect Savior.
The Bible repeatedly exposes human weakness so that divine grace shines brighter.
From Genesis to Revelation, the message remains astonishingly consistent:
This brings us to the heart of the biblical story.
The greatest scandal in history is not human sin.
The Hebrew word חֵן (chen) means grace, favor, undeserved kindness.
In the Greek New Testament, the word becomes χάρις (charis).
A gift that cannot be earned.
A mercy that cannot be purchased.
A love that cannot be deserved.
The entire Bible moves toward the arrival of Jesus Christ.
The Redeemer who would step into humanity's scandal and rewrite it forever.
When Jesus arrived, He consistently moved toward the people society ignored.
The Greek text repeatedly describes Jesus being moved with compassion.
A profound emotional stirring from the deepest part of one's being.
Jesus did not merely tolerate broken people.
Most readers race past names like Eglah.
We hurry toward the stories we recognize.
Yet these names remind us that God's kingdom contains countless faithful people whose impact remains largely unseen.
History often celebrates the visible few.
One day eternity will reveal stories never told on earth.
The Lord who records every sparrow's fall has never misplaced a single faithful life.
Perhaps the greatest lesson from Eglah is that she was never the main character.
The modern world tells us to build our own kingdoms.
Scripture invites us to participate in Christ's.
The modern world tells us to make our names great.
Jesus tells us to make His name great.
The modern world tells us to pursue visibility.
Jesus calls us to pursue faithfulness.
Because in the end, salvation was never found in being remembered by history.
It is found in being known by Christ.
"I know my own and my own know me." (John 10:14)
The Greek word for "know" here is γινώσκω (ginōskō).
It describes intimate, personal, relational knowledge.
Not that the world knows your name.
But that the King of Heaven does.
Maybe Eglah's greatest contribution to Scripture is her reminder that God's story includes people who seem insignificant.
People who occupy only a verse.
People who wonder if they matter.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to save famous sinners.
At Calvary, all stand equally in need of grace.
And at the empty tomb, all who trust Christ receive the same mercy.
That is why the Gospel remains the greatest story ever told.
But because it reveals a Savior who enters human scandal and transforms it into redemption.
A Savior who takes broken stories and rewrites them with grace.
A Savior who takes forgotten people and makes them beloved children of God.
And perhaps that is why Eglah's brief appearance remains preserved forever in the Word of God.
But because she mattered to God.
And if you have ever felt unseen, forgotten, overlooked, or insignificant, remember this:
The God who remembered Eglah has not forgotten you.
The God who saw Hagar sees you.
The God who redeemed David's broken household can redeem your story.
The God revealed in Jesus Christ is still rewriting lives today.
Maybe your name is not known by the world.
But if you belong to Christ, it is written where it matters most.
If this story stirred your heart, do not keep it to yourself.
Have you ever felt unseen by people but seen by God?
The names the world forgets are often the very names God remembers forever.
